title: Composition Series, the Jordan–Hölder Theorem and Solvable Groups

items.title: Subnormal and normal series, factors, refinements, and equivalence
Composition series, composition factors, and composition length
Every finite group has a composition series
items.strategy: Induct on |G|. The trivial group gives the length-zero case. For nontrivial finite G, choose a proper normal subgroup N of maximum cardinality (possibly 1), prove G/N is simple by correspondence, take a composition series of N by induction, and append G. This finite maximization uses no choice principle.

items.title: Dedekind's modular law for subgroup products
items.strategy: For A≤C and B≤G such that AB is a subgroup, prove A(B∩C)=AB∩C by the two inclusions: the forward inclusion is immediate, while x=ab∈AB∩C has b=a^{-1}x∈B∩C. State explicitly that the hypothesis ensuring AB is a subgroup cannot be omitted.

items.title: The Zassenhaus butterfly lemma
items.strategy: For A◁A* and B◁B*, set X=A(A*∩B), X*=A(A*∩B*), Y=(A∩B*)B, and Y*=(A*∩B*)B. Verify X◁X* and Y◁Y* by conjugation and the modular law. Put D=(A∩B*)(A*∩B), use the second isomorphism and correspondence theorems on A*∩B*, and identify both quotients with (A*∩B*)/D to obtain X*/X≅Y*/Y.

items.title: The Schreier refinement theorem
items.strategy: Given subnormal series G=G_0▷⋯▷G_m=1 and G=H_0▷⋯▷H_n=1, refine the interval G_i▷G_{i+1} by G_{i+1}(G_i∩H_j) and refine H_j▷H_{j+1} symmetrically by H_{j+1}(G_i∩H_j). Prove each is a subnormal chain and use the butterfly lemma cell-by-cell to pair its mn factors after deleting repetitions.

items.title: The Jordan–Hölder theorem for groups
items.strategy: Apply Schreier refinement to two composition series. A refinement of a composition series can insert only repeated adjacent terms because each original factor is simple; deleting repetitions therefore recovers the original series. Conclude equal length and a permutation matching the simple factors up to isomorphism.

items.title: The order of a finite group is the product of the orders of its composition factors
items.strategy: Apply the finite quotient-cardinality formula at every adjacent normal inclusion in a composition series and telescope. Mention the trivial group, whose empty product is 1.

items.title: Characteristic subgroups
Characteristic subgroups are normal, and characteristicity is transitive
items.strategy: Inner automorphisms show H char G implies H◁G. If K char H char G, every automorphism of G restricts to an automorphism of H and hence preserves K, proving K char G. Keep separate the false mixed assertion K◁H char G⇒K◁G, which is tested on the companion page.

items.title: The derived subgroup is characteristic and the abelianization is universal
items.strategy: Automorphisms preserve commutators, so they preserve [G,G]; characteristicity supplies normality without appealing to the existing AI-authored normality proof. Use the published quotient-abelian criterion and quotient universal property to prove that every homomorphism G→A into an abelian group factors uniquely through G^ab=G/[G,G].

items.title: The derived series, solvable groups, and derived length
Homomorphisms respect commutator subgroups and derived series
items.strategy: Compute f([x,y])=[f(x),f(y)] to obtain f(G')≤f(G)' and equality when f is surjective. Induct on r to obtain f(G^(r))≤f(G)^(r), again with equality for surjections; specialize to inclusions and quotient maps.

items.title: A group is solvable if and only if it has a subnormal series with abelian factors
items.strategy: If the derived series reaches 1, its successive factors are abelian. Conversely, for G=G_0▷⋯▷G_n=1 with abelian factors, quotient abelianness gives G_i'≤G_{i+1}; inductively G^(i)≤G_i, so G^(n)=1. This also shows the derived series is the fastest descending abelian-factor series.

items.title: Subgroups and quotients of solvable groups are solvable
items.strategy: For H≤G use H^(r)≤G^(r), and for a quotient use surjectivity to identify the quotient's r-th derived subgroup with the image of G^(r). Termination of the derived series then descends in both cases, without a finiteness hypothesis.

items.title: Extensions and finite direct products of solvable groups are solvable
items.strategy: For N◁G with N and G/N solvable, choose r with (G/N)^(r)=1, infer G^(r)≤N, then choose s with N^(s)=1 and show G^(r+s)≤N^(s). Prove (G×H)'=G'×H' directly from coordinate commutators and iterate; derive the finite-product statement by induction.

items.title: A finite group is solvable if and only if all its composition factors are cyclic of prime order
items.strategy: A simple solvable group has nontrivial last derived quotient and must be abelian; a finite simple abelian group is cyclic of prime order by Cauchy's theorem. Thus solvability passes to every composition factor. Conversely, rebuild the group along a composition series using the extension theorem, since prime-order factors are abelian and solvable.

items.title: $A_5$ and $S_n$ for $n\ge5$ are not solvable
items.strategy: Use the published simplicity of A_5 and the published equality A_5'=A_5 to show its derived series never reaches 1. For n≥5, embed A_5 into S_n by fixing the remaining letters; a solvable S_n would have only solvable subgroups, contradiction. Also note directly that A_n is nonsolvable for every n≥5 from the published derived-subgroup computation.

items.title: Subgroup commutators and the lower central series
The upper central series
Nilpotent groups and nilpotency class
Central factors are equivalent to adjacent commutator containments
items.strategy: For N◁G and N≤H≤G, prove H/N≤Z(G/N) iff [G,H]≤N by expanding the quotient commutator. Apply this equivalence to each adjacent pair in a normal series; include the endpoint cases N=1 and H=G explicitly.

items.title: Nilpotence via central series, the upper central series, and the lower central series
items.strategy: Show every central series of length c lies termwise below the upper central series and termwise above the reversed lower central series, using the commutator criterion. Hence Z_c(G)=G iff γ_{c+1}(G)=1 iff G admits a central series of length c; take the least such c to identify nilpotency class.

items.title: Subgroups, quotients, and finite direct products of nilpotent groups are nilpotent
items.strategy: For H≤G, inductively prove γ_r(H)≤γ_r(G). For a quotient map q, prove q(γ_r(G))=γ_r(G/N). For a product, compute γ_r(G×H)=γ_r(G)×γ_r(H) from coordinate commutators. Termination gives the three closure results and the expected maximum bound on product class.

items.title: Every finite $p$-group is nilpotent
items.strategy: Induct on |G|. The published nontrivial-center theorem gives 1≠Z(G); the quotient G/Z(G) is a smaller finite p-group and hence nilpotent. Pull its upper central series back through the quotient map and prepend 1≤Z(G), obtaining an upper central series for G. Treat the trivial group separately.

items.title: Nilpotent groups, and in particular finite $p$-groups, are solvable
items.strategy: Use [H,H]≤[G,H] to prove G^(r)≤γ_{r+1}(G) by induction, so lower-central termination implies derived-series termination. Apply the finite-p-group theorem. This supplies a large, explicit family of solvable groups of small order without importing the later Sylow theory.

items.title: A central extension of a class-$c$ nilpotent group is nilpotent of class at most $c+1$
items.strategy: If N≤Z(G) and G/N has lower-central length c, quotient functoriality gives γ_{c+1}(G)≤N. Centrality then gives γ_{c+2}(G)=[G,γ_{c+1}(G)]≤[G,N]=1. Record that arbitrary extensions of nilpotent groups need not be nilpotent, as the S_3 companion counterexample shows.

title: Composition Series, Solvability and Nilpotence: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Two composition series of $C_{12}$ have the same factors in different orders
items.strategy: Write the subgroup chains C_12>C_6>C_3>1 and C_12>C_4>C_2>1, compute adjacent quotient orders, and identify their factors as C_2,C_2,C_3 in opposite arrangements, illustrating Jordan–Hölder without using any companion-page item.

items.title: A composition series and the derived series of $S_3$
items.strategy: Use S_3▷A_3▷1, identify factors C_2 and C_3, and compute S_3'=A_3 and A_3'=1. Conclude S_3 is solvable of derived length 2 but is not nilpotent because its center is trivial while every nontrivial nilpotent group has nontrivial center.

items.title: Composition and derived series of $S_4$
items.strategy: Use S_4▷A_4▷V_4▷C_2▷1 as a composition series with factors C_2,C_3,C_2,C_2. Compute the derived chain S_4'=A_4, A_4'=V_4, V_4'=1, and compare composition length 4 with derived length 3.

items.title: The dihedral group of order eight is nilpotent of class two
items.strategy: For D_8=<r,s | r^4=s^2=1, srs=r^{-1}>, compute [s,r]=r^2, so γ_2=<r^2> and γ_3=1. Compute Z(D_8)=<r^2>, so the upper series is 1<Z(D_8)<D_8. These matching lengths establish class two.

items.title: The integral Heisenberg group is nilpotent of class two
items.strategy: Present the integral Heisenberg group self-containedly on triples (a,b,c)∈Z^3 with (a,b,c)(a',b',c')=(a+a',b+b',c+c'+ab'). Verify the identity, inverse, and associativity directly, then compute the commutator: only the c-coordinate can remain and every (0,0,c) is central. Hence γ_3=1, while [(1,0,0),(0,1,0)]≠1 makes the class exactly two.

items.title: The composition factors determine a finite group up to isomorphism
items.strategy: Refute with C_4 and C_2×C_2. Both have two composition factors isomorphic to C_2, but one group contains an element of order four and the other does not, so they are not isomorphic.

items.title: Every solvable group is abelian
items.strategy: Use S_3: its derived series terminates after S_3▷A_3▷1, while two transpositions do not commute. The proof is self-contained and cites only A-page definitions and published permutation facts.

items.title: An extension of nilpotent groups is nilpotent
items.strategy: Use 1→A_3→S_3→C_2→1. The kernel and quotient are cyclic and hence nilpotent, but S_3 has trivial center and so cannot be nontrivial nilpotent. Contrast this with the A-page central-extension theorem.

items.title: Every subnormal series is a normal series
items.strategy: In S_4 use S_4▷A_4▷V_4▷< (12)(34) >▷1. Each term is normal in the preceding term, but the order-two subgroup is not normal in S_4 because conjugation relabels its nonidentity double transposition. Thus the chain is subnormal but not normal under the library convention.

items.title: $K\trianglelefteq H\operatorname{char}G$ always implies $K\trianglelefteq G$
items.strategy: Take G=D_8, H=<r> (the unique cyclic subgroup of order four, hence characteristic), and K=<s> after choosing the conventional presentation. Correct the tempting but invalid choice: <s> is not contained in H, so instead use G=Q_8, H=G (characteristic), and any order-four subgroup K, which is normal—also not a counterexample. The authored proof must use the verified S_4 example H=V_4 char A_4 and K=< (12)(34) >◁V_4, where K is not normal in A_4; the strategy records these rejected near-misses to prevent reuse.

title: Free Modules, Exact Sequences, Projective and Injective Modules

items.title: The direct sum of an indexed family of modules
Universal property of a direct sum of modules
items.strategy: For M=⊕_{i∈I}M_i with coordinate inclusions, send a finitely supported tuple to the finite sum of its prescribed component maps. Prove linearity, uniqueness from the coordinate decomposition, and the empty-family case M=0. No choice is used because each input has finite support.

items.title: The free module on a set and its standard basis
Universal property of the free module on a set
items.strategy: Identify R^(X) with the direct sum of copies of the regular module indexed by X. For a set map f:X→M, apply the direct-sum universal property to the maps r↦rf(x). Give the resulting finite-sum formula, prove uniqueness, and include X=∅ explicitly.

items.title: Every module is a quotient of a free module
items.strategy: Apply the free universal property to the identity set map on the underlying set of M. The induced map R^(M)→M sends e_m to m and is surjective because every m is in its image. This construction is canonical and choice-free.

items.title: Invariant basis number and the rank of a free module
Every nonzero commutative ring has invariant basis number for finite bases
items.strategy: An isomorphism R^m≅R^n and its inverse give rectangular matrices A,B with AB=I_n and BA=I_m. If n>m, expand det(AB) using multilinearity in the n columns: every term selects n columns of A from only m positions, so a column repeats and every term vanishes, contradicting det(I_n)=1≠0. Symmetry excludes m>n. This finite determinant proof is choice-free and does not use maximal ideals.

items.title: Exact sequences and short exact sequences of modules
The endpoints of a short exact sequence encode injectivity and surjectivity
items.strategy: Prove exactness of 0→A→B is equivalent to injectivity of A→B by identifying the kernel with zero; dually prove exactness of B→C→0 is equivalent to surjectivity by identifying the image with C. Combine these into the usual characterization of a short exact sequence.

items.title: Split short exact sequences, sections, and retractions
The splitting lemma for short exact sequences of modules
items.strategy: For 0→A--i→B--p→C→0, show a section s of p gives B=i(A)⊕s(C), construct a retraction r of i by decomposing b-s(p(b)), and obtain an isomorphism A⊕C→B, (a,c)↦i(a)+s(c). Conversely extract section and retraction from a direct-sum isomorphism. Prove every implication and uniqueness of the decomposition.

items.title: The abelian group $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ and maps induced by pre- and postcomposition
Covariant and contravariant $\operatorname{Hom}$ are left exact
items.strategy: For 0→A→B→C exact, prove 0→Hom(X,A)→Hom(X,B)→Hom(X,C) exact by image/kernel factorization; for A→B→C→0 exact, prove 0→Hom(C,X)→Hom(B,X)→Hom(A,X) exact by factorization through the quotient. Carry out the elementwise well-definedness checks rather than invoking category theory.

items.title: The injective and surjective Four Lemmas
items.strategy: For a commutative diagram with exact rows A→B→C→D and A'→B'→C'→D', chase an element of ker(B→B') using surjectivity on A and injectivity on C to prove the injective version; reverse the chase using surjectivity on B and injectivity on D to prove the surjective version. State hypotheses adjacent to the relevant conclusion.

items.title: The Five Lemma for modules
items.strategy: In a commutative diagram of two exact five-term rows, apply the injective Four Lemma to the middle map using the left outer epimorphism and its neighboring isomorphisms, and the surjective Four Lemma using the right outer monomorphism and neighboring isomorphisms. State the standard weaker outer hypotheses as well as the all-four-isomorphisms corollary.

items.title: The Snake Lemma for modules
items.strategy: For a commutative diagram of short exact rows, define δ:ker(c)→coker(a) by lifting z through the top epimorphism, applying the middle vertical map, and lifting back through the bottom monomorphism. Prove independence of both lifts, linearity, and exactness at each of the six kernel/cokernel terms by a complete element chase; include the initial and terminal zero terms.

items.title: Projective modules and the lifting property
Free modules are projective, with the exact choice boundary
items.strategy: Given a surjection E→M and a map from a free module R^(X) to M, choose one preimage in E for each basis value and extend by the free universal property. For finite X, finite choice (provable in ZF) suffices; for arbitrary X, this is an application of full AC to the family of nonempty fibers. No countable-choice or dependent-choice principle is invoked as a separate hypothesis.

items.title: Equivalent characterizations of projective modules
items.strategy: Assuming AC where arbitrary free modules are used, prove equivalence of: the lifting property; every short exact sequence ending in P splits; P is a direct summand of a free module; and Hom_R(P,-) is exact. The first, second, and Hom-exactness equivalences are choice-free; P projective implies a free summand choice-free via the canonical free cover, while the reverse direction imports the arbitrary-free projectivity choice boundary.

items.title: Direct sums of projectives are projective, and module categories have enough projectives
items.strategy: Under AC, lift each component map from P_i through a fixed epimorphism and combine the lifts by the direct-sum universal property; this proves ⊕P_i projective. The canonical free cover R^(M)→M then gives enough projectives. Note that a finite direct sum needs only finite choice, while arbitrary families and arbitrary bases use full AC.

items.title: Injective modules and the extension property
Equivalent characterizations of injective modules
items.strategy: Prove equivalence of the extension property, splitting of every short exact sequence beginning in I, and exactness of Hom_R(-,I). Extend the identity along an embedding to obtain a retraction; use a split sequence to extend an arbitrary map; combine with contravariant Hom left exactness. These equivalences are choice-free.

items.title: Baer's criterion for injective modules
items.strategy: The forward implication is immediate by extending maps from left ideals R to R. Conversely, assume every map from a left ideal extends to R; partially order extensions of a given map N→I across submodules of M, use Zorn's lemma to obtain a maximal extension, and if its domain is not M use the left ideal {r:rx lies in the domain} to extend across one more generator, contradiction. This converse uses full AC through Zorn, not merely countable or dependent choice.

items.title: Divisible modules over an integral domain
Over a PID, injective modules are exactly divisible modules
items.strategy: For a PID R, injectivity extends the map rR→D sending r to d and produces x with rx=d, so injective implies divisible without choice. Conversely every ideal is rR and a map rR→D is determined by d=f(r); divisibility supplies x with rx=d, so Baer's criterion gives injectivity. Include R=Z as the abelian-group specialization. The converse inherits Baer's full-AC/Zorn boundary.

items.title: Every abelian group embeds in a divisible abelian group
items.strategy: Let F=Z^(A) map canonically onto A with kernel K. Embed F coordinatewise into the divisible group Q^(A), and map F/K into Q^(A)/K. The kernel is (F∩K)/K=0, while a quotient of a divisible group is divisible. Division of a finite-support tuple uses only finitely many explicit rational divisions, so this construction is choice-free; it also corrects Kleshchev's source typo calling the containing group free.

items.title: Products of injective modules are injective, with the exact choice boundary
items.strategy: For an embedding A→B and map A→∏_{i∈I}I_i, extend every coordinate map A→I_i to B→I_i and combine the extensions into a product map. Finite I needs only finite choice; an arbitrary index set uses full AC to choose one extension from each nonempty set of extensions. Conversely each factor is a direct summand of the product and injectivity passes to direct summands.

items.title: Coinduction sends injective abelian groups to injective modules
items.strategy: For a unital ring R and injective abelian group D, give Hom_Z(R,D) the left R-action (r·φ)(s)=φ(sr). Establish the natural bijection Hom_R(M,Hom_Z(R,D))≅Hom_Z(M,D) by evaluation at 1, with inverse g↦(m↦[r↦g(rm)]). Since the right side extends across subgroup inclusions, the left side does too, proving injectivity.

items.title: Module categories have enough injectives
items.strategy: First give the arbitrary-unital-ring coinduction proof: embed the underlying abelian group of M in a divisible (hence, under Baer, injective) group D, then send m to [r↦j(rm)] in Hom_Z(R,D), with evaluation at 1 proving injectivity. For commutative R, also record Stacks' functorial version: character dual (-)^∨=Hom_Z(-,Q/Z) is exact, evaluation M→M^∨∨ is injective, and dualizing the canonical free cover of M^∨ embeds it in J(M)≅∏R^∨; coinduction and the product theorem make J(M) injective. Full AC enters through Baer and arbitrary products, while the divisible-hull embedding itself is choice-free; countable or dependent choice is not separately used.

title: Free Modules and Exact Sequences: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The standard basis and a universal map from $R^3$
items.strategy: Write e_1,e_2,e_3 explicitly and, for chosen m_1,m_2,m_3 in M, compute the unique linear map R^3→M as (r_1,r_2,r_3)↦r_1m_1+r_2m_2+r_3m_3. Verify uniqueness on the three basis vectors.

items.title: $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is generated but not free as a $\mathbb Z$-module for $n>1$
items.strategy: The residue of 1 generates. Every nonzero free abelian group has a basis element of infinite additive order, whereas every element of Z/nZ is killed by n. Thus generated does not imply free; include the n=1 zero-module boundary separately.

items.title: A regular module with bases of sizes one and two
items.strategy: Let V have countable basis e_0,e_1,… over a field and R=End(V). Define α_0,α_1 by embedding into even and odd coordinates and β_0,β_1 by the inverse projections, so β_iα_j=δ_ij and α_0β_0+α_1β_1=1. The left R-linear maps f↦(fα_0,fα_1) and (g,h)↦gβ_0+hβ_1 are inverse, proving _RR≅_RR^2 and rank failure.

items.title: $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ is projective but not free over $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: Use the idempotent 3 in R=Z/6Z: R=3R⊕(1-3)R and 3R≅Z/2Z, so the module is a direct summand of the free module R and hence projective. It is not free because its cardinality 2 is not 6^n for any finite n, while an infinite-rank free module is infinite.

items.title: $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\times2}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\to0$ does not split
items.strategy: Verify exactness directly. If the quotient map had a section, the image of the nonzero residue class would be an integer x with 2x=0 but x odd, impossible. Equivalently, any retraction r of multiplication by 2 would satisfy 2r(1)=1.

items.title: $0\to A\to A\oplus C\to C\to0$ is canonically split
items.strategy: Use inclusion a↦(a,0), projection (a,c)↦c, section c↦(0,c), and retraction (a,c)↦a. Verify exactness and both splitting identities, then identify the splitting-lemma isomorphism with the identity on A⊕C.

items.title: $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(-,\mathbb Z)$ need not preserve surjections on the right
items.strategy: Apply Hom_Z(-,Z) to the nonsplit sequence 0→Z--2→Z→Z/2→0. Since Hom(Z/2,Z)=0 and precomposition by ×2 acts as multiplication by 2 on Hom(Z,Z)≅Z, the resulting map Z→Z is not surjective. This pinpoints why Hom is left exact but not generally exact.

items.title: Every short exact sequence of modules splits
items.strategy: Refute with 0→Z--2→Z→Z/2→0, reproducing the one-line section obstruction inside this item rather than depending on another B-page item. Contrast with the exact projective-ending and injective-beginning criteria.

items.title: Every projective module is free
items.strategy: Reuse the construction—not the B-page item—of the ideal 3R in R=Z/6Z. The idempotent decomposition makes 3R projective, while cardinality rules out every possible free rank. This distinguishes direct summands of free modules from free modules themselves.

items.title: Every injective module is projective
items.strategy: Use Q/Z as a Z-module. It is divisible and hence injective. If it were projective, it would be a direct summand of a free abelian group; free abelian groups are torsion-free, as are their subgroups and direct summands, but Q/Z is nonzero torsion. Thus it is not projective.
